title: Two conditions, one product: E2 and E1 mechanisms, and what the NMR says
asks: One substrate gives the same product under two sets of conditions. Draw both mechanisms and interpret a clue from the spectrum.

know.h: The reagent picks the mechanism. The same halide can lose HX in one step or in two. A strong base does not wait: it pulls off a hydrogen while the leaving group leaves ({{E2}}). With only a weak base (the solvent), the leaving group must leave first ({{E1}}).

Strong bases to recognize: {{HO-}}, alkoxides ({{CH3O-}}, {{CH3CH2O-}}, {{(CH3)3CO-}}), {{H2N-}}, and hydride {{H-}} (NaH is {{Na+}} and {{H-}}). Weak bases: {{H2O}} and alcohols ({{CH3OH}}, {{CH3CH2OH}}) used as the solvent with nothing added.

{{E2}}: one concerted step, no intermediate, three arrows. Base lone pair to the hydrogen; the C-H bond to the new C=C; the C-LG bond to the leaving group. rate = k[RX][base]. The hydrogen and the leaving group are anti-periplanar.

{{E1}}: two steps. Step 1 (slow): the C-LG bond breaks and leaves a carbocation. Step 2: the weak base takes a hydrogen from a carbon next to the positive carbon, and the C-H electrons form the C=C. rate = k[RX].
The carbocation must be stable for {{E1}} or {{SN1}}: tertiary is good, secondary is possible, primary and methyl never form. A neighbouring benzene ring or C=C stabilizes it by resonance.

{{E1}} and {{SN1}} share the carbocation, so a solvent-only flask always holds some substitution product too: an alcohol in water, an ether in an alcohol. Higher temperature favours {{E1}}, lower temperature favours {{SN1}}.
{{SN2}} never happens at a tertiary carbon (relative rate 0), so a strong base with a tertiary halide gives {{E2}} only. That is why {{NaOH}} with tert-butyl bromide gives the alkene and no alcohol.

On a secondary carbon the pair is {{SN2}} and {{SN1}}: a good nucleophile that is a weak base (such as {{HS-}}) in a polar aprotic solvent attacks from the back in one step and inverts the carbon. The solvent alone (water) lets the leaving group ionize first, and the planar cation is attacked on either face: a racemic product, formed in three steps (ionize, attack, lose {{H+}}).
Tosylate ({{OTs}}) is a good leaving group, like bromide or iodide.

Where the base ends up. In {{E2}} the base leaves bonded to the hydrogen it took: {{H-}} becomes {{H2}}, {{CH3O-}} becomes {{CH3OH}}, {{HO-}} becomes {{H2O}}. In {{E1}} the neutral solvent becomes {{H3O+}} or {{CH3OH2+}}.
The n + 1 rule. A hydrogen with n equivalent hydrogens on the neighbouring carbon appears as n + 1 lines: no neighbours, a singlet; 1, a doublet; 2, a triplet; 3, a quartet; 6, a septet.

Counting signals. Hydrogens in the same environment give one signal, so a very symmetrical molecule gives very few signals. An electronegative atom (O, F) pulls electron density away from the hydrogens near it: they are less shielded and their signal stands apart.

A small extra signal means a by-product. Ask what else the reagent could have done. A strong base can also act as a nucleophile (hydride replacing the halide by H). A solvent can also attack the carbocation ({{SN1}}). Draw the by-product and check that it explains the signal.
Energy diagrams. {{E2}} and {{SN2}}: one hump. {{E1}} and {{SN1}}: two humps with the carbocation in the valley, and the first hump (ionization) is the higher one.

method: Classify the carbon that carries the leaving group (tertiary, secondary, benzylic) and mark the hydrogens on the carbons next to it.
Read each set of conditions and label the reagent: strong base, good nucleophile that is a weak base, or solvent alone.
For the strong base, draw one step with three arrows (E2). For a good nucleophile on a secondary carbon, draw one step with two arrows and invert the carbon (SN2).

For the solvent alone, break the bond to the leaving group first and draw the carbocation. Then draw the second step: the solvent takes a neighbouring hydrogen (E1), or attacks the positive carbon and then loses a proton (SN1).
Write every product of each flask, including what the base and the leaving group became.
Turn the spectral clue into a structure: lines minus one is the number of neighbouring hydrogens, and the number of signals tells you the symmetry. Draw the fragment that fits.
Ask which reagent could have made that fragment and by which reaction, and say why the other flask cannot make it.

pitfalls.h: Drawing a carbocation in the strong-base reaction. E2 has no intermediate: all three arrows go in one drawing.
Using {{HO-}} or {{CH3O-}} as the base in the solvent-only reaction. Only the neutral solvent is in that flask, and it leaves as {{H3O+}} or {{CH3OH2+}}.
Sending the base or nucleophile into a tertiary carbon. SN2 does not happen there.
Starting an arrow at a hydrogen atom or at a positive charge. Arrows start at electrons: a lone pair or a bond.
Reading a septet as seven hydrogens. It is one kind of hydrogen with six neighbours.
Stopping the SN1 mechanism at the protonated alcohol, or drawing only one enantiomer of the product.
